title: Buddy Rich's ear and appetite for new material
summary: Rich could not read music but sensed what was wrong; he had no fixed style, welcomed any chart, and had to play audience favorites.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: But he could tell by looking at it.

He could tell by hearing it. You know we rehearsed the whole thing. He couldn’t read music but he must have had this second sense of the whole picture. For instance you know my CD “On the Wild Side” I recorded “Walk on the Wild Side” the whole suite. I wrote that for Buddy. And he played it but he never got to record it before he died. And when I brought it into him there’s a Dixieland section in there that Elmer Bernstein had in the film. He cut the entire thing out. And I was pissed. But it works that way and so when I recorded it myself I did it the way he wanted it. Because he could tell what the — you know he could tell, all right, by this point the audience is getting itchy. They’re going to want the drum solo, they’re going to want something big. You can’t drag it on after a ballad and have a Dixieland thing. Or whatever. You know, that kind of sense.
Did you ever write a Buddy Rich chart that didn’t have a drum solo that he said, “Okay we’ve got to put in a drum solo.”

Never. And I did a lot of things that weren’t drum solos and he liked them. See one thing about writing for Buddy Rich, I wrote for — I’ve written for the other bands, Buddy did not have a style. People could argue that he did, but he didn’t have a style. You could bring any kind of chart into Buddy and he would try it. He may not like it, he may not use it, but he had a voracious appetite for new material. That’s — my brother Pat hipped me to the fact that never bring anything in two weeks or two months or three months before the recording session. Bring it in at the last minute because he’s tired of that other stuff, he wants new stuff. And for subsequent records I did that, I brought in, you know we were going to record in London and two weeks before we went to London I brought in all that stuff and he said, “All right, let’s go to London and record it.”
So that would get played live maybe a few times before the session. But not too many times.

Yes. Not too many times, because again, he’d get bored. And although he did have his favorites and he had things he had to play like “West Side Story” or “Channel One Suite,” things the audience expected. Like Woody Herman had to play “Woodchopper’s Ball.” You had your little hits and you had to make sure you fulfilled that requirement for the audience. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
